essential: Tommy climbs the filthy house undisturbed. He reasons that 'Mr. Brown' is a password and that entering the meeting room unknown would be foolhardy, then hides in the curtained recess opposite the door, which also overlooks the stairs.

The arrivals, each giving the signal knock: a brutish criminal who answers 'Fourteen' to the bearded, precise-voiced man ('Your number, comrade?'), whom Tommy takes for a German; an Irish Sinn Feiner; a shabby clerk-like man; a working man whose face seems vaguely familiar; and a commanding, well-born man whose face Tommy also half knows but cannot name. Keep the variety, which shows the organisation's reach.

The last arrival is small, pale and gentle-mannered, with Slavonic cheekbones and strange light eyes that seem to see through the curtain. Everyone rises for him. He asks whether Mr. Brown is present and is told only a 'message' has come. He suggests Brown may be among them, and the men eye one another. He is seated as 'Number One'. Number Fourteen shuts the door.

Tommy, shoeless, finds the door locked or bolted. He carefully restores the handle and expresses indignation, then shows his bulldog tenacity: he enters the adjoining bedroom, draws the rusty bolt of the communicating door and listens through a portière. He can hear but not see, so identify speakers only by voice ('rather thought was that of Boris').

Overheard business: the Sinn Feiner demands money for a reign of terror in Ireland. Number One grants it and tells Boris to see to it. The commanding man makes the Belfast quip. There is a loan to an English newspaper, with a Moscow denial if needed. The German reports on the unions 'directed by--Mr. Brown'.
The date of the 29th, set by the Labour leaders, who must believe the strike is their own show. Keep Number One's 'honest men' remarks.
'Clymes must go', assigned to Number Fourteen, with the promise of legal defence and gloves bearing a housebreaker's fingerprints. Keep Fourteen's relish for blood and for jewels in the gutter.

The German admits doubt that the leaders will strike. A certain document would ensure success, but they do not have it and do not know where it is. Perhaps one person knows: a girl. 'This case is different.' The question 'Where is the girl now?' is broken off by the blow from an unseen attacker.
optional: The extended description of the dirt, wallpaper and cobwebs can be cut to one phrase.
The shabby clerk-like man can be reduced to a phrase but should not be deleted, because the later 'He's bluffing you' speaker depends on his presence.

The Irish-American financing exchange ('Mr. Potter', the transatlantic voice, 'money only nominally comes from the States') can be cut as a unit. If cut, also cut the Sinn Feiner's 'thanks to our colleague here' line, or keep it attached to the Belfast quip as a pair.
The German's union details (miners, railways, A.S.E.) can be compressed to one sentence.
The step-by-step handle-turning suspense can be condensed, keeping the locked-door discovery and the 'dirty trick' line.
Tommy's 'Lucky I didn't roll in' reflection can be shortened, but keep the point that he would have given the wrong number.

continuity_checks: The attacker is unidentified. Do not name him or say how he approached.
Speakers heard through the portière are attributed tentatively, since Tommy cannot see them.
The 'German' and 'Russian' labels remain Tommy's inferences.
Mr. Brown's presence stays ambiguous, and no member is identified as him.
Do not name Number One, the familiar faces or the doorkeeper.
The girl is not named Jane Finn in the dialogue, and her amnesia is not explained.
Boris is present and named only through others' speech or Tommy's guess.
risks: Including every arrival may crowd the budget. Compress descriptions rather than drop arrivals, because later identifications depend on them.
title: THE ADVENTURES OF TOMMY
voice_profile: Brisk, comic-thriller third person in a light, ironic 1920s register. In Tuppence's scenes the narrator sits close to her thoughts, wryly reporting her self-congratulation ('intoxicated with the success of truthfulness'), her money-mindedness and her schoolgirl slang. In Tommy's scenes the voice turns slow, practical and understated: he weighs his options, admits to nerves and feels plain indignation ('What a dirty trick!'). Comedy and menace alternate quickly. Short dialogue exchanges carry the plot. Villains give themselves away through tics: snarling, sibilance, heel-clicking. The narrator often inserts small ironic asides and callbacks such as buns, hospital plates and the terrier shake. Characters guess at identities by voice and appearance rather than knowing them.
book_context: Tommy and Tuppence are two demobilised, penniless young people who form the 'Young Adventurers, Ltd.' and blunder into a hunt for Jane Finn and a lost draft treaty. Behind the plot is the unseen 'Mr. Brown', whose rule is to stay as an unnoticed nonentity in the background. The book plants small clues that pay off later: a clerk addressed as Brown, the name Rita, a password, faces that seem familiar, the date of the 29th, a curtained recess, a portrait of the pale Russian. Ignorance is played as accidental bluff: Tuppence 'knows' only a name, and Tommy later fakes knowledge. Chapter II begins the main plot through Tuppence's chance use of 'Jane Finn'. Chapter VIII shows the conspiracy's inner council as overheard fragments, ending on a cliffhanger. Who the leaders and later-named figures are must not be revealed in these chapters.
